topic.angle: Leading digits are not evenly spread

card.title: Why so many numbers start with 1

body.claim: In many real-world lists of numbers, about 30% start with the digit 1, and fewer than 5% start with 9.
body.why: This is Benford's law. In data that spans several orders of magnitude, like populations or river lengths, small leading digits are far more common. It is even used to spot fabricated figures in accounts.

probes.question: In data that follows Benford's law, about what share of numbers start with 1?

image_brief.show: A page of numbers, a ledger or a tax form

claims.claim: About 30% of numbers in many real-world lists start with 1
claims.quote: the number 1 appears as the leading significant digit about 30% of the time
9 appears as the leading significant digit less than 5% of the time

claims.claim: Benford applies to data spanning several orders of magnitude
claims.quote: Benford's law tends to apply most accurately to data that span several orders of magnitude

claims.claim: Examples include populations and river lengths
claims.quote: population numbers, death rates, lengths of rivers

claims.claim: Small leading digits are far more common in such data
claims.note: Implied by the 30% (digit 1) vs under 5% (digit 9) figures quoted above.

claims.claim: Used to spot fabricated figures in accounts
claims.quote: applied for forensic auditing and fraud detection
claims.note: Page also says it is not foolproof; "can help spot" wording is safer than a flat claim.
